items.title: What about a Crystal config file for the compiler?
items.author: HCLarsen
items.content:
It occurs to me that there are some aspects of using the Crystal compiler that would benefit from some customisable options. It wouldn’t need something complex, just a simple text file in your home directory, like what Git uses.

The use case that comes to mind first for me is the generation of new projects. The generated README always assumes that you’re using Github, and it only provides as the username. While it’s not particularly difficult to modify this information, it would be rather convenient to have it auto-populate based on the developer’s preferences.

I’m sure that there are many other options that the community could think of while brainstorming, but this is what I first think of.

Also, I’m aware of , but I find that a config file is a lot cleaner, putting all the information in a single place, than relying on multiple environment variables.

items.title: So how are people actually using this LLM thing?
items.author: Xen
items.content:
To counter the threads about the merits of LLM coding a bit, and make it a bit more practical and, hopefully, inspirational, how about a thread about people using it, and what they’re using? All levels of usage welcome, from “I just paste questions to ChatGPT” to “I got a server burning tokens 24/7 with a multi-agent, multi-model, custom written harness”.

For some reason I started out with OpenCode and Gemini. The latter because I could pull a API token from work. But being an old geezer that tries to avoid having to learn new thing unless hard pressed, I quickly pivoted to running OC as an APC server and using for Emacs as the frontend.

But when OC did the cardinal sin of messing with my workflow (they changed how plan mode worked), I started shopping around. Tried Hermes, but it’s a beast, and I wasn’t sure what the hell it was doing, so I moved on to Pi for a little while.

Lately I’ve been pressured into using Claude Code, which people at work tells me is the best thing since sliced bread.

Being the suspicious old sysadmin type that I am, I’ve locked it down inside a container without access to any of my files, which somewhat limits its magic. A like-minded coworker has produced an MCP server that gives it read-only and sanitized access to our core services (Github, Jira, chat, timetracking and Drive). And as most of our projects utilizes containers, which is difficult to work with from inside one, I ended up getting Claude to code an MCP server it could use to ask to run something outside the container, which pops up a nice prompt in Emacs for approval.

So in usage I just open a session in a project and ask it questions and tells it what to do. Then I review what it did (loosely if it’s just a personal tool, more rigorously when work), before committing.

I don’t let it commit, write commit messages, PR descriptions or anything else meant for human consumption.

Not using any skills, though I’m considering installing Ponytail again.

I’m not to happy about being bound up on Anthropic, but it’s what work has decided to pay for, apart from what we get with our Google subscription. I must admit that Claude seems just a tad more smart than Gemini, but I wonder how much is the model, and how much is the harness. Considering spinning up Pi with Gemini for some comparisons.
